system_prompt:
You are a medical radiology simplification assistant. Convert the following diagnostic radiology imaging report into simple, plain English that the patient and their family can clearly understand (at a 6th-grade reading level).

Rules:
1. Explain the type of imaging scan conducted in simple words (e.g. 'cranial MRI (a detailed brain scan using magnetic fields and radio waves, without any radiation)').
2. Keep essential anatomical and medical terms but immediately explain each in parentheses on first use, e.g. 'cerebellum (the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination)'.
3. Clearly state what was found to be NORMAL first, providing reassurance about unaffected areas.
4. For any ABNORMAL findings (such as lesions, abscesses, ischemia, inflammation, or fractures):
   - Explain what the finding means in plain words without causing unnecessary panic.
   - Explain common terms simply: e.g. 'ischemic-gliotic lesions (tiny microscopic scar spots in the brain caused by reduced blood flow in the past, often seen with aging or high BP)'.
   - Clarify whether the finding is new, chronic, or requires further evaluation.
5. If the radiologist recommends further tests (e.g. follow-up CT, contrast scan, or consultation), state this clearly.
6. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs without bullet points or headers.
7. Preserve all factual observations; never guess, infer, or fabricate findings not in the report.
8. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
user_prompt:
--- Your Task ---
Please simplify the following radiology report into plain English for the patient and family:

Original Medical Report:
BRAIN (CRANIAL) MRI

Clinical information: Headache

Technique: Sagittal and axial T1-weighted; sagittal, axial and coronal FLAIR; axial T2-weighted, DWI, ADC and SWI. (20 ml Dotarem) 3-plane T1-weighted after contrast agent injection.

Findings:

Abscesses are observed in the left parietal lobe, posterior periventricularly located and adjacent to each other, the posterior one measuring approximately 20x18 mm, and the anterior one periventricularly located measuring 18x8 mm and opening into the ventricle, with walls showing contrast enhancement and diffusion restriction in the center. Contrast enhancement is observed in the ependyma extending from the occipital atrium to the body portion of the left lateral ventricle at the ventricle and opening site, and abscess foci showing diffusion restriction are observed within the ventricle and in the occipital horns of both ventricles. Thickening and signal increase not showing contrast enhancement are present in the ependyma in the walls of the right lateral ventricle and 3rd and 4th ventricles and in the cerebral aqueduct. Ventricular system size is normal. Vasogenic edema extending to the corpus callosum is observed in the white matter of the parietal and occipital lobes. Hemorrhage was not detected.

Aside from this, bilateral basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum appear normal.

Main cerebral vascular structures are patent.

Cranial bone structures, both globes, retrobulbar fat tissue, optic nerves, and optic chiasm are normal.

Impression:

· Cerebral abscesses in the left parietal lobe, posterior periventricular location, opening into the ventricle, ventriculitis
· Mucosal thickening in the bilateral maxillary sinuses, ethmoidal cells, and frontal sinuses.
· Minimal inflammatory signal increases in the right mastoid cells.

output_text:
The scan that was done is a cranial MRI (a detailed brain scan that uses magnetic fields and radio waves, and does not use any radiation). It looked at the brain from many angles and also used a special dye (contrast) to make certain areas show up brighter on the pictures.

Everything that was checked in the brain that is usually looked at was normal. The main fluid‑filled spaces inside the brain (the ventricles) are the right size and look normal. There is no bleeding in the brain. The deep parts of the brain that help with movement and coordination (the basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum) look normal. The big blood vessels that bring blood to the brain are open and clear. The bones around the skull, the eyes, the fat behind the eyes, the optic nerves that carry vision to the brain, and the optic chiasm where the nerves cross are all normal.

The scan did find some problems. There are two pockets of infection (abscesses) in the left side of the parietal lobe (the part of the brain that helps with thinking and understanding language). One pocket is about 2 centimeters wide and the other is a little smaller. Both pockets are next to the brain’s fluid spaces (the ventricles) and one of them has even opened into the fluid. The walls of these pockets light up brightly on the scan because of the dye, and the center of the pockets is very dense, which is typical for an abscess. The lining of the fluid spaces (the ependyma) around the left ventricle is also thickened and shows a little more signal on the scan, indicating inflammation. The same lining around the right ventricle, the third and fourth ventricles, and the narrow tube that connects them (the cerebral aqueduct) is also thickened, but it does not light up with dye. The fluid spaces themselves are still the normal size. There is swelling (edema) in the white matter of the parietal and back parts of the brain (the occipital lobes) that extends to the middle part of the brain (the corpus callosum). No bleeding was seen.

Other areas that were checked outside the brain show mild inflammation. The lining inside the two lower sinuses in the cheekbones (maxillary sinuses), the small air cells in the forehead (frontal sinuses) and the cells between the eyes (ethmoidal cells) are a bit thickened, which is often due to a sinus infection. The right mastoid cells (air spaces behind the ear) also show a small amount of inflammation.

Because there are abscesses that have reached the brain’s fluid spaces, this is a serious situation that needs prompt treatment. Your doctor will discuss the next steps, which may include antibiotics, surgery to drain the abscesses, or other treatments. The other sinus and ear findings are usually treated with medications or sometimes a simple procedure. Your doctor will let you know exactly what to do next.
